title: Mechanical Bulls!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the mechanical bull, from the bucking barrel and rodeo training roots to the amusement-era machines, the disputed Bertrand Island claim, and inventor Joe Turner's patent later bought by Sherwood Cryer. They cover how the bull works (spin, pitch, and pistons), how modern units differ, riding tips, and the 1978 film Urban Cowboy, which boosted the bull's popularity via Gilley's bar in Pasadena, Texas. They also discuss Mickey Gilly, the Esquire article, the Saturday Night Fever parallel, Gilley's arson, lawsuits and injuries, and close with listener mail correcting the term "CIA agent" to "officer."
topics: Esquire Ballad of the Urban Cowboy

segments.title: Opening banter on country music and Urban Cowboy
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with reminiscences about 1970s and early 1980s country crossover stars, the shift from outlaw country to pop country, and the link between Urban Cowboy and mechanical bulls.

segments.title: What a mechanical bull is and rodeo roots
segments.summary: The hosts define the mechanical bull as a simulation of rodeo bull riding used mainly for entertainment in bars. They discuss the hazy origins, noting bull riding's roots in Mexican blood sports and the 1930s Rodeo Cowboy Association.

segments.title: Bucking barrel and early machines
segments.summary: The bucking barrel, an oil barrel on a suspended saddle that ranch hands tried to throw riders from, is identified as the precursor to the mechanical bull. The hosts describe safety concerns and the injury risk of riding real bulls.

segments.title: Bertrand Island claim and Joe Turner's patent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a claimed 1930s mechanical bull at Bertrand Island Amusement Park in New Jersey, which they joke about checking via a time machine. They explain that Joe Turner built or held the patent for an early mechanical bull and that Sherwood Cryer bought it for thirty dollars, though Cryer is not the inventor.

segments.title: How the mechanical bull works and modern versions
segments.summary: The machine uses hydraulics with a spin motor and a second motor moving pistons to create pitch, yaw and roll. Older units looked like carnival rides; modern ones use touchscreens, speakers, and inflatable padding. Rental options and prices, including a Buffalo, New York rental and a roughly twenty thousand dollar purchase price, are mentioned.

segments.title: Johnny Utah's and riding tips
segments.summary: Johnny Utah's in New York is discussed, including its bull options and sexy settings. The hosts describe riding tips from pro rider Will Roberts: lean opposite the bull's motion, grip with the thighs, and hold on with the non-dominant hand. The bar-era operators' humiliation-focused role and the surfboard variant are also covered.

segments.title: Gilley's saloon and Mickey Gilly
segments.summary: Sherwood Cryer's tent bar Shelley's in Pasadena, Texas becomes Gilley's, a permanent honky tonk partnered with singer Mickey Gilly, Jerry Lee Lewis's cousin, who had a crossover hit with Looking for Love.

segments.title: Urban Cowboy, Esquire article, and Saturday Night Fever parallel
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the 1978 film Urban Cowboy was based on an Esquire article, whose editor also ran the New York magazine piece behind Saturday Night Fever. They discuss the film's soundtrack, the bar-set plot, and the mechanical bull El Toro as a central prop.
topics: Esquire Ballad of the Urban Cowboy
